Armed Conflict & Security
• Polish authorities opened a terrorism investigation after a gunman killed six people in Krakow’s main square; three additional bodies found at the suspect’s home were identified as family members, with officials citing suspected far-right inspiration.
• Video authenticated by news outlets showed the shooting unfolding in the city’s market square, while Poland declared a period of mourning.
• Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure cut power to hundreds of thousands in Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv, underscoring pressure on the grid ahead of winter.
• In Yemen, the Houthis said at least 33 people were killed in a Saudi air strike amid stalled attempts to reverse a rebel offensive, leaving civilians increasingly trapped.
• Analysts warn antipersonnel mines are resurging in Ukraine and Russia is racing to deploy a Starlink-style network to support long-range drone operations.
Why it matters: Escalating urban attacks in Europe and intensifying infrastructure strikes in Ukraine highlight evolving security threats, while Yemen’s stalemate deepens humanitarian risks and new technologies amplify battlefield lethality.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Israel’s president tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government after inconclusive elections, as parties weigh coalition options that could sideline Benjamin Netanyahu.
• In the U.S., Democrats’ congressional gains and a fractured Republican coalition set up contentious policy battles, including over Trump-era initiatives and Iran policy, as Washington offered a $20m reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program.
• South Africa’s ANC suffered a major setback in local polls, winning around 31% nationally with nearly all votes counted, signaling voter discontent with service delivery and governance.
• The White House signaled a combative communications posture, with Trump urging UFC’s Dana White to become press secretary, while Europe stepped up efforts to reduce tech dependence and China expanded delegate quotas ahead of its 2027 Party Congress.
Why it matters: Fragmented mandates and shifting alliances from Jerusalem to Washington and Pretoria could reshape regional policies on security, trade and technology at a volatile moment.

Society & Human Rights
• Germans are debating the future of Hitler’s destroyed Eagle’s Nest site, weighing reconstruction, abandonment, or reinterpretation amid efforts to confront Nazi memory.
• Heavy rains and flooding in Gaza destroyed thousands of tents and shelters, leaving tens of thousands without cover as civil defense responded to a surge in emergency calls; a mass wedding festival still went ahead for 250 couples.
• Cuba’s widespread power outages and fuel shortages complicate daily life and reporting, highlighting deepening economic strain.
• Paraguay’s ousted president Santiago Peña was charged over a banking collapse that left millions without access to funds, adding a justice dimension to a broad social crisis.
Why it matters: Cultural memory, fragile urban infrastructure, and economic crises are intersecting with human rights concerns in multiple regions, testing resilience and governance.

Sports

• World No. 1 Elena Rybakina withdrew from the WTA Finals due to a virus, with Marta Kostyuk stepping in.
• Australia reached both men’s and women’s Rugby League World Cup finals, overcoming stern challenges from Samoa and Fiji respectively.
• Wales’ rugby union side beat Japan 28-21 but drew scrutiny for an unconvincing performance, while Rangers’ unbeaten run raised questions about missing spark despite strong results.
Why it matters: Star performances and high-stakes tournament advances shape momentum across football and rugby, even as injuries and form guide near-term expectations.

Climate & Environment
• El Niño rains transformed Chile’s Atacama Desert into its largest floral bloom in decades, showcasing a rare burst of biodiversity.
• COP31 opens in Turkey under Australian stewardship after hosting disputes, with debates over ambition, finance, and participation as the US remains absent.
• Environmentalists criticized the Earthshot Prize for holding its awards at a venue tied to a major fossil fuel conglomerate, spotlighting tensions between philanthropy and industry links.
• A cold snap brought unseasonal snow to southeastern Australia, while Sydney’s jacarandas signaled spring in bloom, underscoring climate variability.
Why it matters: From global negotiations to local weather swings and symbolic events, climate actions and optics continue to shape public trust and policy urgency.

• A wearable UV-tracking device prompted renewed attention to sun exposure’s health impacts beyond cosmetics amid heat and high UV events.
• Deep Purple singer Ian Gillan reported positive post-surgery progress, emphasizing rest for full recovery.
Why it matters: Evolving overdose patterns and heat-related risks demand updated public health strategies and education.

Art & Culture

• France’s Prix Goncourt-winning novel revived the story of model Louise Cansot, “the girl of 100 portraits,” whose 1949 murder inspired multiple books.

Why it matters: Global arts institutions are navigating heritage, technology, and representation, reshaping narratives on and off stage.

Why it matters: AI’s rapid diffusion is changing consumer habits, labor markets, geopolitics, and infrastructure policy faster than regulatory frameworks can keep up.

Science & Technology
• Commentary signaled the effective end of Tesla’s Cybertruck as production winds down to prioritize a “Cybercab,” highlighting shifting bets in autonomous mobility.
• NASA opened applications for a new astronaut class to support Artemis, Moon base operations, and groundwork for crewed Mars missions; the agency also announced new Moon base tech and logistics awards.
• Scientists modeled an Earth without life to better distinguish lifeless exoplanets from potentially inhabited worlds, while the public was invited to send names on NASA’s Dragonfly mission to Titan.
• APOD featured a major fireball meteor, capturing public interest in near-Earth phenomena.
Why it matters: Ambitious space plans and advances in exoplanet science move exploration forward as industry pivots reshape the tech landscape on Earth.

Economy & Markets
• Post-midterms, tech and data center projects face mounting public and political scrutiny, with knock-on effects for AI infrastructure financing.
• Apple reportedly saved $2.7bn in taxes by booking profits in Singapore, overtaking Ireland as its chief tax shelter, intensifying debates on global tax policy.
• Anthropic secured a $3.4bn deal to generate gas-fired power for data centers, sidestepping traditional utilities to meet surging energy demand.
• China is set to lead global energy investment in 2026 at an estimated $940bn, while an AI stock slump is reviving interest in overlooked Asian equities; Meta’s $25bn bond sale underscored new dynamics in tech debt markets.
Why it matters: As AI reshapes energy needs and capital flows, regulatory pressure and tax strategies are redefining corporate playbooks and investor positioning.

Art & Culture.title: South Korea’s Médongaule Modern Garden Turns Nietzsche Into Pavilions, Paths and a Maze
Art & Culture.text: SummaryMédongaule Garden has opened its Modern Garden in Yangpyeong, South Korea, the second phase of a 14-year plan to build the country’s first humanities gardenChilean studio Pezo von Ellrichshausen designed the pavilions while French landscape architect Guillaume Gosse de Gorre shaped the plantingWalkways built from salvaged stone, waste concrete and preserved dead trees turn the grounds into a route through philosophy and historyMédongaule Garden has opened its Modern Garden in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, a landscape that translates the ideas of Nietzsche and a roster of other thinkers into architecture, planting and circulation. The new grounds arrive 14 years after the project began and build on the site’s Korean Garden, which opened in September 2025. Together, they push the destination toward its goal of becoming the country’s first dedicated humanities garden.Where the Korean Garden reworked a traditional garden culture that was cut off by the colonial era and industrialization, the Modern Garden layers a Nietzschean framework on top and opens the conversation to a global audience. The site is organized along two axes. The “Island of Thought” interprets thinkers including Nietzsche, Plato, Saint-Exupéry, Kazantzakis, the Buddha and Levinas through buildings, walking routes and sightlines, and it is meant to send visitors away with new questions rather than fixed answers. The “Story of Korea” landscapes the country’s arc from a nation of scholars through industrialization and democratization to the present, so a personal stroll becomes part of a shared national memory.Chilean studio Pezo von Ellrichshausen, whose work has been shown at MoMA and the Venice Architecture Biennale, designed the Über House and the garden’s main pavilions. The studio’s buildings are placed to coexist with the terrain instead of dominating it, keeping the landscape as the main event.The planting comes from Guillaume Gosse de Gorre, a French landscape architect from a family line of garden makers. He visited Korea every season during the design process, studying the angle of the sunlight, the movement of the wind and where each plant would settle. His approach is clearest in the meadow garden, a 25,000-plant field that changes completely from season to season. Korean landscape architect Lee Jae-yeon oversaw the landscaping across both the Korean and Modern Gardens, grounding the international vision in local terrain and sensibility.The paths carry as much meaning as the buildings. The infinity-shaped “Eternity” mosaic path is pieced together from stones that would otherwise have been thrown away. The “Era of Overcoming” walkway reuses waste concrete in its raw state, and the “Era of Hardship” forest trail deliberately keeps its dead trees standing. Across all three, natural material, time and history become one design vocabulary.The Über House sits at the garden’s highest point and takes its name from Nietzsche’s Übermensch, giving visitors a full view of the grounds from the summit. Below, a maze garden runs without any signage, so getting lost becomes part of the reflective experience.The Über House also hosts FATI, a restaurant led by chef Lee Dong-hee, coach of Korea’s national culinary team. The kitchen serves modern Korean food built on a garden-to-table philosophy, using produce grown on site. Médongaule is also launching an annual membership that covers both gardens and adds preview events, docent programs, seasonal content, and food and merchandise perks. The garden plans to add performances, exhibitions and academic programs in the future.Médongaule’s Modern Garden is open daily except Mondays, with more details available on the official website.Médongaule’s Modern Garden1 Medeonggol-gil, Yangdong-myeonYangpyeong-gun, Gyeonggi ProvinceSouth Korea,Opening hours: 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Batman to Bond? Robert Pattinson Reportedly Screen Tested for 007
Entertainment.text: SummaryRobert Pattinson is among the actors who have screen tested to play James Bond, according to 'The Hollywood Reporter'He reportedly joins a shortlist that includes Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and possibly Nicholas HoultThe casting search is the first under Amazon, which took creative control of the franchise from the Broccoli family in February 2025Robert Pattinson has reportedly screen tested to play James Bond, making the 40-year-old Batman star the most famous name yet linked to Amazon’s search for the next 007. Multiple sources told The Hollywood Reporter that Pattinson read for the part alongside fellow hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor.According to THR, the tests took place over the weekend of October 24 in London, where Pattinson is currently filming The Batman Part II. The outlet had previously reported that four or possibly five actors were in contention, though only three names had surfaced at that point. Nicholas Hoult is now said to be another contender, which would set up a rematch of sorts, since Hoult finished as runner-up to Pattinson when the Batman role was cast years ago. Amazon declined to comment on the screen tests.Pattinson’s inclusion cuts against the long-held assumption that the next Bond would be a rising name rather than an established global star. He is one of the most prominent actors of his generation and already fronts DC Studios’ Batman franchise, which makes him an unusual fit for a role that has typically gone to someone audiences can grow into.The strongest link may run through Denis Villeneuve, who is directing the next Bond film. Pattinson worked with the filmmaker on Dune: Part 3, which arrives December 18, and the collaboration is said to have gone well for both of them.Pattinson has built his résumé around ambitious directors, working with Robert Eggers, the Safdie brothers and Christopher Nolan, whose 2020 espionage thriller Tenet now looks like an unofficial dry run for 007. This year has been his strongest yet, with a key role in Nolan’s The Odyssey, a co-lead turn in the A24 hit The Drama and the lead in A24’s well-received Primetime.The franchise itself is in uncharted territory, as this will be the first Bond film made under Amazon, which bought creative control from the Broccoli family in February 2025. Spider-Man producer Amy Pascal and Harry Potter producer David Heyman are steering the project. The Heyman connection stands out, since Pattinson first broke through with a tragic role in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, a few years before Twilight made him a worldwide name.The search comes 21 years after Daniel Craig was announced as Bond in October 2005. Craig played the role across five films before stepping away with 2021’s No Time to Die, a run that included 2012’s Skyfall, the only film in the franchise to cross $1 billion USD.Stay tuned for more details.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Gorsch’s FW26 “The Dancing People” Collection Is Cut for Movement and Built From Rare Cloth
Entertainment.text: SummaryGorsch’s Fall/Winter 2026 offering, titled “The Dancing People,” closes out the second half of the Iwate label’s fourteenth seasonDesigner Eiichi Suzuki mixes rare deadstock fabrics with custom and locally made textiles across a run of unisex cutsHighlights include a black flannel cape coat and a denim set colored with kakishibu, a dye made from fermented persimmon tanninGorsch has unveiled “The Dancing People,” its Fall/Winter 2026 collection, a lineup of outerwear, shirting and trousers from Iwate-based designer Eiichi Suzuki that puts fabric and fit ahead of everything else. The season completes the second chapter of the Japanese label’s fourteenth season, leaning into heavy flannels, a signature herringbone and a persimmon-dyed denim set built around how clothes behave on a moving body.Suzuki’s design language falls somewhere between vintage work garments and proper tailoring, but the cuts are engineered for everyday ease rather than period costume. Every piece is drawn as unisex, with proportions intended to sit well on a broad spread of body types. The fabric strategy follows the same thinking, pairing hard-to-find deadstock cloth with textiles developed specifically for the brand and others produced locally.This season’s direction comes from movement, with Bazar Cirque performers Ken Sakagami and Aoi Kagaya, both friends of the label who perform in Iwate, shaping the collection and fronting its campaign, which was shot in the prefecture by photographer Atsushi Meguro and styled by Suzuki himself. That brief translates directly into the build, with dense, cushy fabrics, oversized proportions and a weighty drape that swings when the wearer moves and settles cleanly when they stand still.The Flannel Wool Cape Coat in black anchors the outerwear, while the most technically interesting piece is a denim set colored with kakishibu, a dye made from fermented persimmon tannin. The set pairs a Short Length Jacket with matching Two Tuck Trousers, giving the dye treatment a full head-to-toe canvas.Elsewhere, the Brushed Collar Wide Shirt arrives in an off-white linen-wool blend, and the trouser offering runs deep. The Wool Two Tuck Trousers come in black flannel as well as the collection’s Dynamic Herringbone weave in navy and terracotta, with the Flannel Wool Easy Trousers in brown rounding out the lineup.Gorsch’s FW26 “The Dancing People” selection is available now at Standard & Strange’s stores in New York, Berkeley and Santa Fe, as well as online via the retailer’s website.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Adam Driver Confirms He Is Done Playing Kylo Ren
Entertainment.text: SummaryAdam Driver says he will not return as Kylo Ren, closing the door on the shelved standalone film 'The Hunt for Ben Solo'Driver and Steven Soderbergh spent several years developing the project before Disney’s top executives turned it downFans campaigned to save the film with billboards and a banner flown over Walt Disney Studios in BurbankAdam Driver has ruled out playing Kylo Ren again, saying The Hunt for Ben Solo, the standalone Star Wars film he developed with Steven Soderbergh, is no longer in play. Asked on a recent episode of The Rich Eisen Show whether he could see himself returning as the character, Driver said, “Yeah, it’s over… No more ‘Star Wars.’”The project began as a long-term collaboration between Driver and Soderbergh, who was attached to direct. Over several years, the pair worked on a screenplay together with writers Scott Burns and Rebecca Blunt, building a story around Ben Solo as the lead of his own film. Driver told Eisen the group put serious effort into the script and that he thought the result was strong.Lucasfilm was on board at first. Driver has previously said the studio responded well to the pitch and understood the angle the team was taking. The project stalled once it reached Disney’s top leadership, when CEO Bob Iger and Alan Bergman declined to move forward because they could not see how Ben Solo, who dies at the end of the sequel trilogy, could plausibly be alive. Driver summed up the decision to Eisen by saying the executives told him the character was dead.Once the news became public, fans responded on a large scale. Supporters paid for billboards and hired a plane to fly a “Save The Hunt for Ben Solo” banner over Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, California. Driver said he was surprised and moved by the scale of the response, especially the billboards and the plane over Disney’s lot.None of that changed the outcome. Soderbergh signaled in April that the film would already have happened if it were going to, and Driver’s latest comments go further. Pressed by Eisen on whether he would come back if someone revived the project, Driver said that would be up to the studio, not to him or Soderbergh, before adding, “I think the ship has sailed though.”Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: BEAMS’ “DEAR VINTAGE COLLECTION” Dresses the 2026 MAMA AWARDS in Band T-Shirt Nostalgia
Entertainment.text: SummaryBEAMS teams up with CJ ENM’s 2026 MAMA AWARDS on the DEAR VINTAGE COLLECTION, a line of official merchandise for the eventThe graphics draw on vintage band tees, festival shirts and corporate promotional teesThe six-piece lineup covers a logo T-shirt, game shirt, zip-up hoodie, tote bag, cap and bandanaBEAMS has partnered with the 2026 MAMA AWARDS on the DEAR VINTAGE COLLECTION, official merchandise for CJ ENM’s awards show, taking place on November 20 and 21. Instead of standard event merch, the Japanese retailer has based the range on the graphic styles of collectible vintage tees.The design approach draws on three familiar kinds of printed tee. Band shirts, music festival tees and corporate promotional shirts all serve as references, so the MAMA AWARDS logo is treated less like event branding and more like a find from a vintage rack. The result is merchandise meant to be worn well after the show is over.Apparel makes up half of the lineup. A logo T-shirt anchors the collection, a game shirt brings in a sports-uniform cut, and a zip-up hoodie adds a heavier layer for the winter event dates. Each carries the collaboration’s MAMA AWARDS branding in the vintage-inspired graphic style.The other three pieces are accessories that carry the same graphic treatment at a smaller scale. A tote bag, a cap and a bandana complete the six-piece offering, giving fans lower-commitment ways to pick up the collaboration alongside, or instead of, the apparel.The BEAMS x 2026 MAMA AWARDS DEAR VINTAGE COLLECTION will be available via the BEAMS official online store, BEAMS Namba and the official 2026 MAMA AWARDS MD booth.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The Overlay-Free Nike Air Max 90 SP “Black Leather” Receives a November 2026 Release Date
Entertainment.text: Name:  Nike Air Max 90 SP “Black Leather”Colorway: BlackSKU: IV4504-001MSRP: $170 USDRelease Date: November 13Where to Buy: NikeThe Nike Air Max 90 SP “Black Leather” now has a firm release date, with the pared-down take on the classic runner set to arrive on November 13. Part of Nike’s Fall 2026 slate, the pair swaps the silhouette’s signature layering for a mostly leather build defined by stitching instead of stacked panels.With the date locked in, the focus turns to how different this pair looks from a standard Air Max 90. A typical version builds its shape from leather, mesh and plastic pieces layered on top of one another, but this release handles nearly everything in leather. Rather than adding separate overlays, Nike uses stitch lines to trace the Swoosh, the mudguard and the side panels. Each element stays readable against the black, while the overall surface ends up noticeably flatter and cleaner than the model’s usual profile.Perforated leather takes over the areas that normally use contrasting materials. The plastic eyestays are gone, replaced with punched leather that sits flush with the rest of the upper, and the same material wraps the heel, where Nike has dropped the usual Nike Air branding. A tonal logo on the tongue is the only obvious mark left, and black laces disappear into the upper instead of breaking up the colorway.All of the reworking stops at the sole. The familiar Air Max 90 midsole and visible heel Air unit carry over unchanged, finished in black along with the rubber outsole. The one break in the dark palette is a faint blue tint inside the Air window. The stripped-back result sits closer to the minimal styles NikeLab has released over the years than to a typical Air Max 90.Set your reminders and get ahead of what’s dropping next on Hypebeast Drops.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: New Arrivals From HBX: Moncler
Entertainment.text: Brand Information: Moncler is an Italian luxury brand founded in 1952 by Réné Ramillion in the French alpine village, Monestier-de-Clermont. Over the past six decades, Moncler has cemented itself as a pioneer in the field of functional outerwear. The world-famous outerwear label is especially well-known for its trademark quilted down jackets. In 1968, Moncler designed the professional team uniform for the French alpine skiing team at the Winter Olympics in Grenoble. Today, under the current president and creative director Remo Ruffini, Moncler stands strong as a global lifestyle brand that develops urbane and masculine styles of quilted down jackets, vests, parkas, knit accessories, and even casual wear like T-shirts, sweatpants, and tipped polo shirts.  By using patent fabrics and fur details, Moncler injects a modern feel to heritage looks, whilst combining extreme warmth with day-to-day city life.
